title: String Methods
description: Built-in tools for measuring, cleaning and reshaping text.

content.value: Strings are not only for showing on screen. Every string in Python comes with a set of tools attached to it, and you reach them by writing a dot after the text, then the tool's name and a pair of parentheses. Tools that work this way are called methods.
One measuring tool is written differently. `len()` wraps around the string rather than following a dot, and it counts every character, including spaces and punctuation.

message = "Hello World"

print(len(message))      # 11: five letters, a space, five letters
print(message.upper())   # HELLO WORLD

`.upper()` turns every letter into a capital and `.lower()` turns every letter small. `.title()` capitalises the first letter of each word, which is handy for tidying up a name somebody typed in a hurry.

name = "aDA loVElace"

print(name.upper())   # ADA LOVELACE
print(name.lower())   # ada lovelace
print(name.title())   # Ada Lovelace
Lowercasing is the usual trick for comparing what a user typed. `answer.lower() == "yes"` is True for "yes", "Yes" and "YES" alike, which saves writing a condition for every spelling.

`.strip()` removes spaces from the very start and end of a string, and leaves the ones in the middle alone. It is worth using on anything a person typed, because a stray space at the end is invisible and still breaks a comparison.

typed = "  yes  "
print(typed == "yes")            # False, because of the spaces
print(typed.strip() == "yes")    # True
`.replace()` swaps one piece of text for another. You give it two things: what to look for, and what to put in its place. Every match is swapped, not just the first.

sentence = "I like apples and apples"
print(sentence.replace("apples", "cookies"))
# I like cookies and cookies

Here is the part that catches people out. A string method never changes the string it was called on. It builds a new string and hands that back, leaving the original exactly as it was. So calling a method on its own line achieves nothing at all.

message = "hello"

message.upper()        # the result is built, then thrown away
print(message)         # still hello

message = message.upper()   # store it to keep it
print(message)         # HELLO
If a string method seems to do nothing, check whether you stored the result. Either use it straight away inside a `print`, or assign it back to the variable.

print(secret.strip().upper())

quiz.question: Which tool gives the number of characters in a string?
quiz.explain: len() counts the characters, spaces included. It wraps around the string rather than following a dot.

quiz.question: What does  "  hi  ".strip()  give you?
quiz.explain: .strip() removes the spaces at the start and end only. Spaces in the middle of the text are left alone.

quiz.question: What is printed?  message = "hello"  /  message.upper()  /  print(message)
quiz.explain: The capitals were built and then thrown away, because the result was never stored. message itself never changed.
